study: Epistemic Boundary Mimicry / Go qualification pilot

source.source_text:
Corda workshop calls its thin laminated test panels foldglass. A bench notebook by Maro Pell, dated September 2019, compares their shape after movement between a damp room and a dry room. The workshop uses these panels as experimental samples rather than approved building components. Each sample carries an inked identifier that remains attached throughout the sequence.

The notebook follows 24 panels in four shallow trays, with 6 panels in each tray. The observers keep the tray supports and room lamps unchanged. They move whole trays rather than spray individual panels. After three hours in each room, they photograph each identified sample beside the same square-grid reference card. The card supplies a visual reference, not a reported angle measurement.

After the damp-room period, 16 panels have their free edges visibly raised; the remaining 8 have no clear change in the photographs. The notebook does not identify the unresponsive samples as a separate manufacturing batch. Its comparison concerns edge shape, not the appearance of a new coating or a different ink label.

On the next day, 7 responsive panels undergo a damp-to-dry-to-damp sequence. All 7 flatten and then raise their edges again in that order. Brief removal from a room for photography does not immediately erase the observed shape. The recorded sequence covers two days and supports reversibility only over that observed interval.

The author proposes unequal moisture uptake across the laminated layers as a working explanation. Room transfers alone do not isolate that mechanism from temperature drift or handling effects. The notebook treats these as unresolved alternatives and warns that judging an edge from a photograph can depend on camera position.

No internal-layer microscopy was performed. No outdoor-weather exposure trial was conducted. The team did not test repeated cycling over several weeks.
